notes.meaning: The writer's heart bubbles over with excitement as he composes a song for a royal wedding. The Holy Spirit guides his tongue just like an expert writer uses a pen. While he writes for an earthly monarch, his poem ultimately celebrates King Jesus and His kingdom.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some early church teachers took the first line as God the Father speaking about the eternal generation of His Son, while the prompt writing describes how quickly God sent Christ into the world.

notes.meaning: The king is praised for having unmatched charm, and his words are filled with pleasant grace. God has poured out His favor on him so that he will enjoy lasting blessings. In a deeper way, this describes the beauty of Christ's character and the life-giving words He speaks to sinners.

The poet urges this royal champion to strap his sword to his side and get ready for action. He is called to display true majesty and splendor, which belong to God but are shared with His chosen king. For Christians, this points to Jesus taking up the sword of His word to conquer evil.

The king rides out to battle not for selfish glory, but to defend truth, humility, and fairness. His own skilled right hand will lead him to accomplish great and awesome deeds. In the same way, the gospel of Christ advances quietly and powerfully across the world, winning hearts without human cruelty.

The king shoots sharp arrows straight into the hearts of his enemies, bringing opposing nations to their knees. These arrows picture God's word when it strikes the human conscience with deep conviction of sin. Sinners are brought down in repentance so they can be saved and reconciled to God.

The throne of this ruler is declared to stand forever, and his royal staff guarantees total justice. The New Testament quotes these exact words to prove that Jesus is God the Son, who reigns over an unending kingdom. His rule brings perfect fairness because evil has no place in it.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars translate this line as 'your divine throne' or 'God is your throne,' viewing it as the grand poetic language of ancient royal courts rather than a direct statement that the earthly king is God.

notes.meaning: The ruler loves what is right and truly detests wickedness. Because of this pure character, God has anointed him—setting him apart with special oil—giving him greater joy than any other ruler around him. This points to Jesus being filled with the Holy Spirit and exalted to the highest place of gladness in heaven.

The king's wedding clothes are scented with precious spices like myrrh, aloes, and cassia. Beautiful music from stringed instruments welcomes him as he steps out of palaces decorated with polished ivory. These sweet scents reflect the pleasing virtues and holy life of Christ our Savior.

Royal daughters are among the honored guests at court, and the bride stands at the king's right hand in the place of highest honor. She wears the finest gold brought from the distant land of Ophir. This scene shows the great value Christ places on His church, treating His people as His treasured bride.

The poet speaks like a wise counselor to the young foreign bride, urging her to listen carefully. She must let go of her old attachments, leaving behind her native people and her father's household. In the Christian life, believers must leave behind worldly loyalties to give their full devotion to the Lord.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: The Eastern Orthodox Church sings this verse as a sacred hymn during special feast days honoring Mary, the mother of Jesus.

notes.meaning: When the bride devotes herself completely to her husband, the king will truly delight in her beauty. She is told to bow before him and show him honor as her lord. This reminds the church that Christ takes great pleasure in His people, and that He deserves our worship and joyful obedience.

People from Tyre, a famous and wealthy seaport city, bring lavish gifts to honor the new queen. Even the richest and most powerful people seek to win her favor. This pictures nations from all across the world turning to Christ and bringing their best treasures to serve His kingdom.

The royal bride looks glorious inside her bridal chamber, dressed in a gown woven with pure gold thread. Her outward splendor matches the dignity of the royal household she now belongs to. For believers, this points to the inner beauty given to the soul by God's grace, making His church lovely in His eyes.

The bride is led to the king in colorful, embroidered robes, accompanied by a joyful train of bridesmaids. They enter the royal palace with cheering, music, and great gladness. This procession represents the wonderful day when Christ's people are finally brought into His heavenly presence with everlasting joy.

The poem turns back to the king with a promise that his sons will take the place of his ancestors. He will appoint these children as leaders and princes over the land. In the gospel, this looks ahead to Christ bringing many spiritual children to glory, raising believers up to share in His heavenly reign.

The writer vows to keep the king's memory alive across all generations to come. Because of the king's great deeds, nations far and wide will praise him forever and ever. God fulfilled this promise by preserving this song, ensuring that believers everywhere will praise Jesus for all eternity.
